topic: Chemistry — Structure and bonding of carbon
subject: combined-science

items.q: In diamond, how many covalent bonds does each carbon atom form, and with what?
items.correct: Four covalent bonds, with four other carbon atoms
items.misconception: Four covalent bonds, to atoms of other elements
items.why: Students reason that two substances with such different properties cannot be made of the same thing, so they assume something extra must have been added to diamond. Both are carbon; only the bonding differs. Four bonds per atom in three dimensions gives diamond, three bonds per atom in layers gives graphite.
items.random_wrong: Four covalent bonds, inside a small molecule

items.q: Which set of properties does diamond have?
items.correct: Very hard, very high melting point, does not conduct
items.misconception: Very hard, low melting point, does not conduct
items.why: Students meet covalent bonding first in small molecules such as CO₂ and carry the 'covalent means molecular, so weak forces between molecules' rule straight over to diamond. Point out that no molecule can be found in diamond: the covalent bonds run right through the whole crystal. There is nothing between molecules to overcome, so the covalent bonds themselves must be broken.
items.random_wrong: Very hard, very high melting point, conducts electricity

items.q: Explain why diamond has a very high melting point.
items.correct: Many strong covalent bonds have to be broken to melt it
items.misconception: The weak forces between diamond's molecules must be overcome
items.why: Students meet covalent bonding first in small molecules such as CO₂ and carry the 'covalent means molecular, so weak forces between molecules' rule straight over to diamond. Point out that no molecule can be found in diamond: the covalent bonds run right through the whole crystal. There is nothing between molecules to overcome, so the covalent bonds themselves must be broken.
items.random_wrong: The delocalised electrons hold the carbon atoms in place

items.q: Explain why diamond does not conduct electricity.
items.correct: All four outer electrons of each carbon are in bonds
items.misconception: Covalent bonds between its layers stop electrons moving
items.why: Diagrams of graphite draw dotted or faint lines between the layers to show the stacking, and students read those lines as bonds. Read the specification wording: layers of hexagonal rings which have no covalent bonds between the layers. If covalent bonds joined the layers, the layers could not slide and graphite could not mark paper.
items.random_wrong: Its delocalised electrons cannot move through the structure

items.q: In graphite, how many other carbon atoms is each carbon atom bonded to, and how are the atoms arranged?
items.correct: Three others, in layers built from rings of six carbon atoms
items.misconception: Four others, in layers built from rings of six atoms
items.why: 'Carbon always makes four bonds' is a rule students learn early and apply everywhere. Graphite is the exception they must hold in mind alongside it. Tie the number of bonds to the delocalised electron. Carbon still has four outer electrons in graphite, but only three go into bonds; the fourth is the one that is delocalised.
items.random_wrong: Three others, in a giant three-dimensional network

items.q: What does the specification say about bonding between the layers in graphite?
items.correct: There are no covalent bonds between graphite's layers
items.misconception: Strong covalent bonds join each layer to the next
items.why: Diagrams of graphite draw dotted or faint lines between the layers to show the stacking, and students read those lines as bonds. Read the specification wording: layers of hexagonal rings which have no covalent bonds between the layers. If covalent bonds joined the layers, the layers could not slide and graphite could not mark paper.
items.random_wrong: The delocalised electrons form covalent bonds between layers

items.q: How many electrons from each carbon atom in graphite are delocalised?
items.correct: One electron from each carbon atom is delocalised
items.misconception: All four of the outer electrons of every carbon atom
items.why: Students transfer the metal picture wholesale - positive ions in a sea of electrons - and assume every outer electron joins the sea. Only the electron left over after the three covalent bonds is delocalised, so it is one per carbon atom. Three of the four outer electrons are still held in bonds.
items.random_wrong: Two electrons from each atom, leaving 2+ ions in the sea

items.q: Explain why graphite is soft enough to leave a mark on paper.
items.correct: Layers slide off because no covalent bonds join them
items.misconception: Its covalent bonds are weak, so the structure crumbles
items.why: Students link 'soft' straight to 'weak bonds'. Because graphite rubs off onto paper they assume whatever holds it together must be feeble, and they never separate the bonding inside a layer from what is between the layers. Ask where the sliding happens. It happens between the layers, where the specification says there are no covalent bonds. Inside each layer the covalent bonds are strong, which is why graphite still has a very high melting point.
items.random_wrong: Its delocalised electrons let the carbon atoms slide past

items.q: Explain why graphite conducts electricity.
items.correct: One delocalised electron per carbon atom can move through it
items.misconception: Its carbon atoms move along the layers carrying charge
items.why: Students take the whole metallic bonding model across at once instead of the single feature the specification names. The similarity the specification asks for is the delocalised electrons, and that is all. Graphite is built from carbon atoms held by covalent bonds, not from positive ions.
items.random_wrong: Ions in graphite are free to move between the layers

items.q: In what way is graphite similar to a metal?
items.correct: It contains delocalised electrons that are free to move
items.misconception: It can be hammered into new shapes without breaking
items.why: Students take the whole metallic bonding model across at once instead of the single feature the specification names. The similarity the specification asks for is the delocalised electrons, and that is all. Graphite is built from carbon atoms held by covalent bonds, not from positive ions.
items.random_wrong: It is held together by strong ionic bonds, as metals are

items.q: What is graphene?
items.correct: A single layer of graphite, exactly one atom thick
items.misconception: A stack of several graphite layers bonded firmly together
items.why: 'Thin' is easier to hold on to than 'single layer', so students settle for a few layers rather than exactly one. The specification defines graphene as a single layer of graphite. One layer, not a few; that is the whole definition.
items.random_wrong: A hollow ball of carbon atoms, like Buckminsterfullerene

items.q: Graphene is useful in electronics. Which explanation of this uses graphene's structure and bonding correctly?
items.correct: It conducts: each carbon has a delocalised electron
items.misconception: It conducts, because its weak covalent bonds free the electrons
items.why: Students link 'soft' straight to 'weak bonds'. Because graphite rubs off onto paper they assume whatever holds it together must be feeble, and they never separate the bonding inside a layer from what is between the layers. Ask where the sliding happens. It happens between the layers, where the specification says there are no covalent bonds. Inside each layer the covalent bonds are strong, which is why graphite still has a very high melting point.
items.random_wrong: It does not conduct: all four outer electrons are in bonds

items.q: Which statement about Buckminsterfullerene is correct?
items.correct: It is a hollow, spherical molecule with the formula C₆₀
items.misconception: It is a giant covalent structure with the formula C₆₀
items.why: All the other forms of carbon in this topic are giant structures, so students expect fullerenes to be giant too, and the word 'carbon' triggers the giant covalent answer automatically. A giant structure is a continuous network with no separate molecules, so its formula only gives the ratio of atoms - carbon itself is written C. A fullerene is a separate molecule, and C₆₀ counts the atoms in one of them. That is why fullerenes have hollow shapes and definite sizes.
items.random_wrong: It is a solid ball of carbon, with the formula C₆₀

items.q: A structure is described as a hollow cage of carbon atoms built from hexagonal rings together with some rings of five carbon atoms. What is it?
items.correct: A fullerene, as its cage can contain rings of five atoms
items.misconception: Graphene, because a graphene sheet is a hollow carbon cage
items.why: Graphene, fullerenes and nanotubes are met in the same lesson as 'the new carbon structures', and the striking football image of C₆₀ attaches itself to whichever name is being asked about. Anchor graphene to graphite, not to fullerenes. Peel one layer off graphite and you have graphene - it is flat and open, not closed into a cage.
items.random_wrong: Diamond, because its rings can hold five carbon atoms

items.q: Which description fits a carbon nanotube?
items.correct: A cylindrical fullerene with a very high length to diameter ratio
items.misconception: A solid rod of pure carbon with a very high length to diameter ratio
items.why: The word 'tube' is read as 'rod' or 'wire' once students picture nanotubes reinforcing materials or carrying current, and the fullerene link is forgotten. The specification calls nanotubes cylindrical fullerenes, and every fullerene is hollow. The carbon atoms lie in the wall of the tube; the inside is empty.
items.random_wrong: A sphere of carbon atoms with a very high length to diameter ratio

items.q: Which of these is a use of fullerenes, including carbon nanotubes?
items.correct: Strengthening composites and use in electronics
items.misconception: Cutting and drilling hard rock, as they are the hardest
items.why: All the other forms of carbon in this topic are giant structures, so students expect fullerenes to be giant too, and the word 'carbon' triggers the giant covalent answer automatically. A giant structure is a continuous network with no separate molecules, so its formula only gives the ratio of atoms - carbon itself is written C. A fullerene is a separate molecule, and C₆₀ counts the atoms in one of them. That is why fullerenes have hollow shapes and definite sizes.
items.random_wrong: Lining furnaces, as they melt at a very high temperature

items.q: Does diamond conduct electricity?
items.correct: No. Diamond does not conduct electricity, because all four outer electrons of every carbon atom are used in covalent bonds and none is delocalised.
items.misconception: The different forms of carbon are interchangeable, so diamond and graphite have the same structure and properties (for example, each conducts electricity).
items.why: Diamond and graphite are taught together as forms of carbon, so students generalise the property of one to the other, sometimes helped by knowing that diamond does conduct heat well. Compare the bonding, not the element. Graphite conducts because each carbon uses only three of its outer electrons in bonds, leaving one delocalised. Diamond uses all four, so it has no delocalised electrons.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Where are diamond's delocalised electrons?
items.correct: Diamond has no delocalised electrons at all. Every outer electron of every carbon atom is in a covalent bond.
items.misconception: Diamond has delocalised electrons, but they are trapped and cannot move.
items.why: Students remember 'no conduction' and invent a reason that keeps the electrons: they picture delocalised electrons that are somehow stuck, rather than accepting that there are none. Count the electrons. Carbon has four outer electrons and forms four bonds in diamond, so four out of four are used. Nothing is left over to be delocalised.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does graphite have a high or a low melting point?
items.correct: Graphite has a very high melting point, because melting it means breaking the many strong covalent bonds within its layers.
items.misconception: Graphite has a low melting point because its layers slide over one another so easily.
items.why: Students merge two separate properties: sliding layers make graphite soft, and softness feels like something that would melt easily. Separate the two questions. Sliding needs nothing to be broken, so graphite is soft. Melting needs the strong covalent bonds inside the layers to be broken, so the melting point is very high.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which rings are found in fullerenes?
items.correct: The structure of fullerenes is based on hexagonal rings of carbon atoms, but they may also contain rings with five or seven carbon atoms.
items.misconception: Fullerenes are built only from hexagonal rings, exactly like graphite layers.
items.why: Fullerene structures are introduced straight after graphite, and the hexagon is the shape students have just been drilled on, so the five- and seven-membered rings are dropped. A sheet of hexagons alone stays flat. The rings of five, and sometimes seven, are what let the sheet curve round and close into a hollow shape.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What carries the current when a solid conducts electricity?
items.correct: In graphite and in metals the current is carried by delocalised electrons moving through the structure.
items.misconception: Only ions that are free to move can carry an electric current, so a solid without ions cannot conduct.
items.why: The rule 'ions must be free to move' is learned for molten and dissolved ionic compounds and is then applied to every conducting substance. Ions are not the only charge carriers. Graphite contains no ions at all, yet it conducts, because one electron from each carbon atom is delocalised and free to move.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
